subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Coffee Rust Catastrophe
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Coffee Rust Catastrophe.

hook.text: Ceylon was the world's top coffee exporter in 1870. Within 20 years, the industry was dead.

buildup.text: Coffee leaf rust—a fungus called Hemileia vastatrix—arrived in 1869 and spread across every plantation.

discovery.text: The fungus produces orange spores under leaves that kill the tree's ability to photosynthesize.

twist.text: Planters ripped out coffee and planted tea instead. That's why Sri Lanka is famous for tea today.

climax.text: Coffee rust still costs Latin America over $1 billion per year. It remains the crop's worst enemy.

punchline.text: A fungus turned a coffee island into a tea island.

quiz.question: Why is Sri Lanka known for tea instead of coffee?
options: Coffee rust destroyed all coffee plantations in the 1870s–1880s

details.summary: In the 1870s, coffee leaf rust devastated plantations across Asia, destroying the coffee industry of Ceylon and much of Southeast Asia. The disaster pushed Ceylon into tea production, redirected global coffee trade toward the Americas, and demonstrated how disease can reshape an entire industry.
details.whyItMatters: The coffee rust catastrophe was a turning point in global agricultural history. It destroyed one continent's coffee industry and made another continent dominant.
takeaways: Coffee rust destroyed Ceylon's coffee industry in the 1870s
It pushed Asian coffee regions toward tea production
The Americas became dominant as Asian production collapsed

faq.question: What happened to Ceylon after coffee rust?
faq.answer: Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, pivoted from coffee to tea production. The transition was painful but ultimately successful. Ceylon became one of the world's premier tea-producing regions, a legacy that persists today. The switch demonstrates how agricultural crises can redirect entire national economies.

faq.question: Is coffee leaf rust still a threat today?
faq.answer: Absolutely. A devastating outbreak hit Central America in 2012, destroying up to 40 percent of production in some countries. Climate change is expanding rust's range to higher altitudes. Breeding resistant varieties is a top priority for coffee research institutions worldwide.
